title: A few who play otherwise: marked mutants in a world of equals

thesis.claim: A world of equals holds against a few who play otherwise. A line whose brain is changed in 1,000 of its numbers leaves fewer copies there than a line left as it is; a line changed in 10 numbers, the step that world mutates by, leaves as many.
thesis.why: With half its agents given other brains a world of equals lost most of its tokens to them (Experiment 59), yet it lasted 4,500 iterations while one copy in five was changed in 10 numbers (Experiment 53). So it should resist deviants while they are few: in a world where every node is won by the coalition of all its stakers, a brain that stakes otherwise is outweighed on every node, and one that keeps its tokens at home or has a child gives up its share of its neighbours' nodes. A change of 10 numbers alters about one decision in a hundred and should cost nothing; a change of 1,000 alters a fifth to two fifths.
thesis.confirm: In each of the two worlds, 100 mutant sites and 100 control sites are marked in each of eight assays of 9 iterations. R is the mean count of the mutant sites after six iterations over that of the control sites, pooled over a world's eight assays, and its range is that of 95% of 2,000 shufflings of the labels within each assay. In both worlds: R for 1,000 numbers lies below its shuffled range, and R for 10 numbers lies inside its own.
thesis.refute: In both worlds R for 1,000 numbers lies inside its shuffled range or above it: a few who play otherwise do as well as the rest. Anything else is undecided. Reported beside it: R for 100 numbers, R after three and after nine iterations, and the share of lines still alive.
